name: Safe zones for pins or screws in the humeral shaft
corridor: Anterolateral deltoid window in the proximal third (protecting the axillary nerve), no percutaneous corridor in the middle third, and a posterior or open-lateral window in the distal third that visualizes the radial nerve

positioning.text: Support the arm so proximal-lateral and, if the patient is not strictly supine, posterior distal pin sites can be imaged. In a supine polytrauma patient the posterior distal corridor is usually inaccessible.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the acromion (axillary nerve about 5–7 cm distal), the deltoid insertion, and the olecranon fossa. There is no percutaneous safe zone in the middle third.

incision.text: Use a formal incision large enough to palpate or see the nerve. Do not use stab incisions, especially if a distal pin must sit laterally near the radial nerve.

superficial_interval.text: Proximally go (antero)laterally through deltoid, avoiding the axillary nerve and long head of biceps. Distally the classic corridor is posterior through triceps; if a lateral pin is forced by positioning, open enough to see the radial nerve.

deep_interval.text: Advance pins so the tips just perforate the far cortex. Do not place pins in the middle third. Distally stay out of the olecranon fossa.

layers.text: Skin, deltoid or triceps, periosteum, then humeral cortex, with the axillary or radial nerve identified before drilling.

structures_at_risk.text: The axillary nerve and long biceps tendon proximally, the radial nerve on the middle and distal dorsal shaft, and the median nerve and brachial artery if a distal pin is driven too deep, are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The middle third has no percutaneous safe zone because the radial nerve hugs the dorsal cortex. Over-penetration medially threatens the neurovascular bundle. Distal over-penetration threatens the median nerve and brachial artery.

retraction_hazards.text: A posterior distal pin can irritate the triceps and make bed positioning uncomfortable; if a lateral pin is chosen instead, visualize the radial nerve rather than retracting blindly.

exposure.text: Each site is only a pin window. The distal-humerus page recommends a mini-open technique whenever humeral pins are required.

limitations.text: The posterior distal corridor is usually unavailable in a supine polytrauma patient. The middle third cannot be pinned percutaneously.

indications.text: Used when external-fixator or percutaneous pins must be placed in the humeral shaft through defined proximal or distal corridors.

closure.text: Close the mini-open windows after confirming the nerve is free of the pin.

complications.text: Complications include axillary-nerve injury, radial-nerve palsy from a middle-third or unseen lateral pin, and median-nerve or brachial-artery injury from an over-long distal pin.

procedure_applications.condition: Temporary external-fixator pins are placed in the humeral shaft

questions.question: Is there a percutaneous safe zone in the middle third of the humerus?
questions.answer: No. The radial nerve is too close to the dorsal cortex.

questions.question: How far below the acromion does the axillary nerve typically run?
questions.answer: About 5–7 cm, dorsolaterally around the metaphysis.

questions.question: If a distal pin must be placed laterally in a supine patient, what is required?
questions.answer: An incision large enough to palpate or see the radial nerve; no stab incisions.
